speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I would like to say a few words on this motion.
We are asked to reduce the quorum from 13 to nine members. The committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts is made up of 25 members of parliament.
I feel that there is something wrong. If 13 members out of those 25 cannot be found to attend that committee's sittings, then I submit that the committee is not important and must cease its activities.
The first point I want to make is that the Ralliement Creditiste is not represented at all on eight committees because the Liberals refused to allow us a member on them. An attempt was made to divide the number of committee members according to the number of members in each party.
It is a fact that Liberal members are not interested in taking part in the work of committees. On the other hand, we are interested and, in spite of that, there are eight committees on which the creditistes are not represented at all. It is not surprising, therefore, that committees fall short of the quorum when interested members are not allowed to sit on them.
And on how many committees is the party of my hon. friend the member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) not represented? And if I
asked the same question to the members of the New Democratic Party? They are also interested in sitting on committees where they are not represented. I am convinced that there would be many of them if they were invited to become members of those committees.
They cannot attend because they were denied that. There are members of the New Democratic Party and the Ralliement Creditiste who are not members of the committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts and who, in spite of that, attend its sittings. There is for instance, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). I do not think he is a member of that committee and yet he attends its meetings although his attendance is not recorded. Why? Because there is no room for those who are interested. Members of the Liberal party are chosen even if they are not interested and do not show up. Then, there is no quorum. Those who are interested cannot make up the quorum. That is my first argument.
Mr. Speaker, hon. members who are interested, whatever their party, should be asked if they want to sit on committees and should be allowed to do so if they agree. Then we would have a quorum and the committees could hold their meetings. If at least members who are interested could have their names substituted for those who have given their names to be members of committees, but are not interested.
There are hon. members who are interested in being members of this committee, but are not. Why? Because there is no room for them. When I asked the member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) the other day whether he would have liked to sit on the committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts, he said he would have accepted. At any rate, he attends the meetings, but he is not a member of the committee and his presence does not count for the quorum. There is a weakness in the establishment of committees. The Liberal whip has to run after his own members to get them together, to ask them to attend committee meetings, even when they are not interested. The situation is the same for the Conservative party.

Broadcasting Committee
Instead of leaving that to the whips, all members interested in being members of a given committee should be asked to give their names. Afterwards, the substitutions needed could be made. Thus, we would not be faced with the problem we have today.
The second reason why I object to the quorum being reduced from 13 to nine is that no committee is without Liberal members, none has less than 13 Liberal members. If the government is serious,-it is to the government that we owe the committee reform________
it should see to it that all members of its party attend committee meetings. There are 13 Liberals on each committee, but they are not interested in attending the meetings. That is why there is no quorum. The party in office wants to have too big a share in committee membership. Its members are not interested; they do not want to take part in committee meetings and that is why there is no quorum.
Mr. Speaker, I submit that if the members of the party in office were interested in attending committee meetings, then we would not face the problem we face today and there would be a quorum in committees.
As the motion is debatable and as we are entitled to 30 minutes each, I intend to use all my time or at least a good deal of it, because I believe that we are now debating a question of principle dealing not only with the committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts, but to any other committee. What is good for one committee is good for all the others.
The third reason why I strongly object to reducing the quorum is because I found that when a committee has a hard time getting a quorum, it is because more important work is being carried out in the house. For instance -and the chairman of the committee can bear me out on this point-Monday and Tuesday last, the committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts found it hard to get a quorum for certain sittings. Why? Because important speeches were being delivered in the house, namely a statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), which was awaited by everyone. Now, it was understandable to find all Liberal members present in the house. That same afternoon, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) made an important speech and Conservative members were present in great numbers in the house. In the evening a very important vote took place. That is why the committee on broadcasting, Aims and assistance to the arts did [Mr. Gregoire.l
May 9, 1986
not have a quorum all day long. This is entirely normal and I am convinced that the Prime Minister preferred making his statement when all members of his party were present in the house instead of making it in front of empty seats or when members of his party were scattered here, there, and everywhere in various committees.
It is quite understandable, Mr. Speaker, that members should be present in the house when important matters are being discussed here. But then, committees cannot get a quorum.
Mr. Speaker, the main reason is that committee members are selected by the whips, whereas all members, regardless of their party, interested in taking part in committee work should be able to do so.
The second reason is that counting the government members there would be enough for a quorum, but they are not interested.
In the third place, there is the fact that when something important is happening in the house, members prefer to sit in the house rather than in the committees, and that is perfectly normal. But reducing the quorum would not solve the problem because in that case, when members have to choose between a committee in which they are particularly interested and the house, where something important is happening, what would their decision be?
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
What should we, as members, choose? We are faced with a difficult alternative. The member should not be given such an alternative. He has to choose between being absent from committee meetings which are important and which, he feels, he ought to attend, and being absent from the house while something important is going on. A member should not be faced with such an alternative.
That is why the solution is not in reducing the quorum but in a better organization of the committees' work, in finding a system whereby members may be allowed to attend the house when it is important and also to attend the committee sittings when such committees, also of importance, are sitting.
Such a formula must be found instead of reducing the quorum.
We are asked to reduce the quorum to nine, which means that only nine members would submit reports and decide on some matters on behalf of all their colleagues. That is not proper.
May 9, 1966

Let me give an example. During the debate on the budget speech in the house, the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs was sitting. Now, the people most interested in the budget debate are necessarily the members of the finance committee. Yet, the finance committee was sitting during consideration of the budget in the House of Commons. That is not proper. Those who are interested in the financial administration of the country had to choose between taking part in the budget debate, which lasted six days and which is surely the most important debate of the session on financial matters, and attending the committee sittings where consideration was being given to the financial problems of the country.
You see, Mr. Speaker, the situation in which members interested in the problems and financial administration of the country found themselves. They could not be in both places at the same time while discussions were taking place on important matters concerning the finances of this country. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I claim that the solution is not in the reduction of committees' quorum but in finding time periods during which the committees could sit outside the sittings of the House of Commons. For instance let the house sit three weeks a month and let the committees sit one week while the house is not sitting.

maintopic: BROADCASTING, FILMS AND ASSISTANCE TO THE ARTS CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Or three days a week.

maintopic: BROADCASTING, FILMS AND ASSISTANCE TO THE ARTS CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Or yet, have the house sit three days per week and, as the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) suggests, allow the committees to sit two days a week while the house is not sitting.
Let the committees sit a week per month or two days per week, while the house is not sitting, and their work will be done more seriously. Besides, members could then attend the sittings of the House of Commons. The way things are being done at the present time we would have to be in both places at the same time and that is not possible.
We are still looking for the scientist who will discover a system allowing people to be in two places at the same time. Such a system has not yet been developed and it is not this government which will develop it either. We still do not possess the gift of ubiquity. For lack of this system for the time being, we cannot be forced to be in the house and in the committees at the same time.
Broadcasting Committee
I therefore ask the government and the leader of the house to devise another system, different from that which is offered to us at this time.
That is why we object to the motion before us today.

maintopic: BROADCASTING, FILMS AND ASSISTANCE TO THE ARTS CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can agree with many of the things the hon. member for Lapointe has said. However, I plan to support this motion because it is the only way out of our immediate difficulties. But I would suggest that a committee of representatives from each party should be formed to discuss these matters.

maintopic: BROADCASTING, FILMS AND ASSISTANCE TO THE ARTS CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: A committee on committees.

maintopic: BROADCASTING, FILMS AND ASSISTANCE TO THE ARTS CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
A committee on committees, if you like.
I do not believe we are going to settle this matter on the floor of the house each time one of these motions comes before us.
I should like to make one suggestion, Mr. Speaker. It seems to me that the house might well consider a system of appointing alternate members to committees. Quite frequently a committee has to meet on Monday and a member has not returned from his riding. If his party were able to name an alternate, that member could be there to take his place and it might be possible to provide a quorum. There have been many times, as the hon. member for Lapointe has said, when there have been enough members at committee meetings but not members named to the committee. It seems to me that this is a suggestion which might help to provide quorums and get the committee sessions under way. I would like to suggest again that this matter is not going to be settled in the house, but that a committee dealing with committees should take this matter under advisement very soon.

maintopic: BROADCASTING, FILMS AND ASSISTANCE TO THE ARTS CONCURRENCE IN FIFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should also like to protest the suggestion that quorums of committees be reduced. I have found in any organization in which I have previously been involved that only a few people participate actively in the real work of the organization. However, I believe in this particular situation in the House of Commons we are only a few-265 representatives-of the 20 million people who elected us. I believe the people of Canada have the right to expect that their representatives will concern themselves with

May 9, 1966
Broadcasting Committee the business of the nation, and that concern should be a continuing one as long as this house is in session.
It might be a good idea to recall the situation which brought about the hearings of the committee on broadcasting. The intention was to debate the whole issue on the floor of this house, but rather than use the time of the house when we have so much other business to attend to the suggestion was that the matter should be turned over to the standing committee on broadcasting. It seems to me that those who favoured the plan to turn it over to committee and those who opposed this plan have a common interest in seeing that a quorum for the committee is maintained, and that we should take the committee work seriously. I will agree that it is not a good thing to see the press and witnesses waiting for hours for a quorum to develop, but I do not believe there would be any improvement if the membership of the committee is reduced to nine when the membership of the entire committee is 25. If we have to reduce it to as low as nine we will be throwing out the balance which a committee should have in hearing the important issues placed before it.
How can such a committee possibly have the temerity to ask witnesses to come from great distances and from important duties to present their case to such a small group of members of parliament? I cannot see any witness looking at us very favourably under such circumstances. I would suggest that we take our duties a little more seriously than we have been doing, and that the alternatives which have been suggested by previous speakers be considered and tried before we act on the easy suggestion of reducing the size of the quorum.

Mr. Speaker, I sincerely believe that the hon. member for Lapointe is right in asking that the quorum be left as it is. If the Liberals cannot take their responsibilities concerning the committee in question, they should not lay the blame on the others; let them attend the meetings and the other members will also attend, as they are doing now.

One of those reasons is that, not so long ago the house voted an increase in parliamentary indemnity, and the people would not look kindly upon an apparently unexplainable measure to reduce the quorum of the committees.
By the way, Mr. Speaker, I am not so sure that the committee is truly overworked, because in my own personal case and in the case of some of my colleagues, I know that we are members of three committees that have been convened only twice in the past four months. We surely can handle more than that.
There may be another reason, deeper than that mentioned by some of my colleagues. Reading the newspapers and magazines, we have heard, we have read recently that there were in the house and in all parties, members called the "Young Turks" who are complaining that they are not kept sufficiently busy
Broadcasting Committee and are not carrying enough responsibility. I think it would be sound psychology to give them work to do and keep them occupied in committees.
Mr. Speaker, I think the crux of the matter is to find means to get members to attend the committees. There are several. I think the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) mentioned one worthy of consideration when he spoke of television. At these committee sittings, when members realize that the roll is called in front of television cameras and that their constituents will see they are absent without valid reason, they will then probably want to attend more often.
Accordingly, I shall second the proposal made by the hon. member for Lapointe.

Mr. Speaker, I believe it is quite evident to the members of the committee which designed the rule changes that some modifications are necessary in these rules. I believe if we reduce the quorum of this committee now to nine we will have to reduce it again in a matter of a week or two to five. We are increasing the number of committees that are meeting, and I think this must be taken into consideration. The answer to the problem really is not a reduction of the quorum, but rather to persuade the members of committees that the committees are worth attending. Then arrangements should be made so they can attend those meetings.
I think this is a matter which concerns the house, and it certainly concerns the house leaders. There are 16 committees now constituted. The meetings of these committees have to be carefully arranged so they can get a quorum and the members will find it possible to attend meetings. The reduction in quorums might solve the problem for the government temporarily, but it really does not solve the problems of the committees and make it possible for them to work properly.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
The question of consideration of the estimates is also affected. We agreed to give the committee procedure a fair shake for a year to see whether we could overcome the problems. We are not doing this now because we are asking for a reduction in quorums and this eliminates the government's responsibility in connection with this matter. I suggest this procedure does not give the new committee procedure a fair chance. It is up to the house leader to call a meeting of committee

May 9. 1968
Broadcasting Committee members and representatives of the other parties in order to reduce all quorums. If half the members is too much then let us reduce it to one third. I think it is unfair to the country, unfair to members of parliament, yes, and unfair to the operation of the committees themselves to reduce the quorums unless they are reduced for all other committees.
The actions of some committee members have strangled the committees. When members hedge-hop from one committee to another the proceedings have to be started over again, and I think it is the government's responsibility to make sure that the system works. However, to reduce this quorum, without reducing the quorums of other committees, is to continue a bad situation. I suggest that this type of motion ought not to be introduced now by the chairman of a committee. Instead, I think the government ought to consider revising the committee structure that does not seem to work. The number of members necessary for a quorum should be decided, but we should avoid doing it in the haphazard way that has developed.
The present system does not seem to work. It should therefore be overhauled. I think anything less is not fair to members of parliament, and would not be fair to the rule changes that were made to correct the way things were going.

before the motion carries I should like to say a few words.
Personally, I would not object to it, nor vote against it, because this request is only made for a limited time, this week.
Since the committee will not sit before eight o'clock tonight, we shall only miss one sitting of the house.
Mr. Speaker, the request made this afternoon by the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Pelletier) shows that, once more, our whole committee system is poorly organized. We are asked to sit while the house is sitting. However, if we consider the business of the house for today and tomorrow only, we see for instance, that the house will be asked to vote on the setting up of the new Department of Manpower.
Thus, 50 or 60 members about will be called to sit on committees while the house is discussing matters as important as the setting up of a Department of Manpower, of a Department of the Solicitor General and the creation of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, as well as the setting up of a Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development which will replace that of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
That is less important, Mr. Speaker; this would be the exception to the rule. While that department is being set up, very well, we can sit on the committees, but very important things will happen and, in spite of all that, some members will have to attend committee meetings.
That clearly shows, Mr. Speaker, that our committee structure is not up to date, that reforms are needed.
I think that the committee on the business of the house, which is under your chairmanship, Mr. Speaker, should convene to find a better procedure with regard to the creation and organization of committees.
The hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury) said a short while ago that the attendance of the members of his party, or at least his own party in the house, was relatively good compared to that of the other parties. I am glad he did not give any statistics, because he would have found that he 
was talking through his hat and was not too well aware of the situation, because I remember one day when our party, although allowed only one member on a committee, had two and sometimes three members attending meetings and asking questions, which means that our party had three times as many members as it was entitled to, whereas some of the hon. member's colleagues who had been appointed members of that committee were not there. ABANDONMENT OF BURNED OUT TRAWLER
speechtext: Did H.M.C.S. Gatineau leave the burned out fishing trawler Karen B after the crew abandoned her on April 1, 1966, before the arrival of the Halifax-based tug Foundation Vigilant and. if so. for what reason?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: ABANDONMENT OF BURNED OUT TRAWLER
speechtext:
1. The circumstances pertaining to the fishing trawler Karen B were as follows: On 1 April, 1966, fire broke out on board the Karen B, which was approximately 100 miles off Halifax. A distress message was sent and the crew of 14 took to a life raft. Two Sea King helicopters were promptly dispatched from Canadian forces base Shearwater and the crew of 14 and a dog were picked up and flown to Shearwater.
H.M.C.S. Gatineau, which was at sea, was diverted to the position of the Karen B. When she arrived, later in the day, the fire was out and the Karen B was out of danger. Having ascertained that the trawler was seaworthy, that a Canadian salvage vessel was on its way, and that there were no other ships within 20 miles of the Karen B, the Gatineau resumed operations.

As was demonstrated in this instance, the navy responds immediately to any emergency at sea and takes all possible action to save lives and property. The navy does not normally involve itself in salvage operations, however, leaving this to salvage companies who derive their revenue from this type of work and strongly object to the navy becoming involved in salvage operations thereby establishing claim by naval personnel to salvage entitlements.

Mr. Speaker, I direct my question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. As 36 African states have this action in mind and as it was a result of Canada's action that many of these states found their way into the United Nations, what is Canada's stand on this question? subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am very pleased to be able to move the adoption of this resolution, item No. 56 on the order paper, which stands in my name. In doing so I think I can say, with general agreement, that the legislation contemplated in this resolution will be very important indeed in the conduct of government. The purpose of the resolution as set out in its opening words is:
-to introduce a measure respecting the organization of the government of Canada-
In moving the motion for the adoption of the resolution, I want to talk primarily about the purpose and the need for reorganization of government as proposed in the resolution. Then, Mr. Chairman, if the resolution carries, I shall be pleased to go into the matter in much greater detail on second reading of the bill.
The reorganization of administrative responsibilities which the government has undertaken, which is referred to in this resolution and which will be reflected in the proposed bill if the resolution is adopted by the house, constitutes the most extensive change in the administrative organization of government that has ever been made in peacetime. I am afraid we have had a tendency to ignore or at least, if not to ignore, to under-estimate, the importance of the administrative organization in achieving the substantial results which we expect from policies, results which are vital at a time when government is far more concerned with and is far more important to the life of the citizen, the productivity of our economy and indeed the character of our society, than has ever been the case before.
I put alongside the desirability, indeed, the necessity of reorganizing our parliamentary procedures to make parliament a more effective instrument in agreeing on policies, the necessity for that change to adapt parliamentary institutions to the needs of our contemporary society, the parallel need of reform in
Establishment of New Departments the administrative organization of government so that government as such will be able to achieve the substantial results and maximum effectiveness which we expect when policies are adopted by parliament. Results both in policy and in administration are vital, as I say, at a time when the government is so concerned not only with making the national economy work but with protecting and advancing the interests of the individual.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
We are well beyond the point where it is even a matter of debate whether government should assume any responsibility for economy planning, for social adjustment, for individual welfare and for the basic nature of our society. All countries now recognize that effective organization and administration in government are an essential part of the complex inter-relationships that are a feature of our technical and rather affluent society.
If the role of policy making is vital, and it is, it is equally vital that administration should be well conceived and efficiently directed. Indeed, effective administration and organization lie at the core of many of our political problems. The reorganization which is now being undertaken and which is referred to in this resolution will, I believe, contribute in an important way to the effectiveness of government administration in important areas of national activity in the years ahead.
The broad outlines of the measures contemplated in this resolution are already known. Many of the proposed bills' more immediate objectives have already been implemented, as has been done in the past in similar circumstances, by the use of the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act. Certain statutory changes are required to establish fully, formally and finally the new and the affected departments. The names of several departments have to be altered to reflect their new functions. It is interesting to note that while under the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act it is possible, because parliament has given government this authority and power, to transfer duties in a very important way without further legislation, it is not possible, except by legislative change, to alter the name of a department. That is only one reason why, of course, legislation is required. Also, in some cases departmental structures have to be fitted to different roles and some legislation is required for this. The reorganization that I mention, Mr. Chairman, will, I
4872	COMMONS
Establishment of New Departments believe, facilitate more effective action in a number of important areas of government responsibility.
I have been glad to note that there has been widespread public approval of the changes that are being proposed. I believe this approval stems from public recognition of the changing needs of our times and the changing demands on government to meet those needs, and also that the structure of government be adapted to meet those needs.
The recent report of the Economic Council of Canada states in endorsing one important change, and I quote from the report:
The area of greatest need for urgent and effective action is that of manpower and labour market policies . . . whether an active manpower policy is to be successful hinges critically on effective administration.
And the report goes on:
It is essential that a proper administrative structure be established for co-ordinating labour market programs. This is an important initial step.
Along with the Economic Council, the government recognizes, in the words of the report, and I quote again:
That the development of strong initiatives and effective policies to promote adaptability and mobility of the labour force, to facilitate the matching of demand and supply of labour, and to generate timely and useful information about labour market conditions, will yield high rates of return in relation to the resources required to implement them.
That is one change that is being proposed, Mr. Chairman, the setting up of a ministry which will deal with manpower problems.
The government has also decided that it would be a wise course to place immigration under the same minister as the minister dealing with manpower generally. Immigration policy obviously must be administered in the interests of the country and of the immigrants themselves in a context that takes into account the entire position of employment, training and placement in Canada. The association of the various aspects of manpower policies under the same minister should make it easier to implement programs and to implement them more effectively.
As hon. members know, the department of manpower will be in addition to and not be a replacement for the Department of Labour. The latter will continue its traditional and important role in conciliation and labour relations, in the field of labour standards and labour conditions generally. These are very important functions, especially in times of remarkable economic activity such as the

present and of increasingly rapid change in the techniques of production that so affect, as they are affecting now, the position of labour. So there will be a very important role for the Department of Labour to continue to play.
It has become increasingly difficult for one minister to discharge fully both areas of responsibility at the present time. I speak of manpower on the one hand and labour relations on the other. With the attention of two ministers, one in the area of labour relations and the other in the area of manpower, placement and training, we will be in a better position than we were before to deal effectively with two of the most important aspects of our economy in the present climate of great domestic activity and high international competition.
A third department, Mr. Chairman, that bears directly on employment opportunity, productivity and the standard of living, is forestry, which the government organization bill seeks to have renamed and enlarged as the department of forestry and rural development. This change will recognize the increasing importance of the department's responsibilities for the government's program in agricultural rehabilitation and development. The program already extends well beyond agricultural matters to include a variety of instruments aimed at breaking what has been called in the Economic Council's report, from which I again quote:
-the vicious circle of low productivity, low incomes, low government revenues and low investments in growth-promoting services.

Before I apologize to the committee perhaps the right hon. gentleman will allow me to try to find out the reason for the omission. This is, I believe, in the resolution: the government will continue to recognize the special regional development problems of the Canadian north through a department of northern development. Under the government organization bill, however, Indian affairs replaces national resources as the companion responsibility of the minister of northern affairs.
As the royal commission on government organization pointed out, the joining together of Indian affairs and northern development is a natural step which cannot but strengthen both the well-being of Canada's indigenous peoples and the cause of northern expansion and development. The new organization will place under one minister federal responsibility for both the Indian and the Eskimo people. This change will result in more effective work than has hitherto been possible and will help to eliminate differences in standards and treatment which have been a cause of some criticism and discontent.
The resource jurisdiction which has been connected with the development of the north will remain under the minister of northern development. Other resource responsibilities once located in the department of northern affairs have now been transferred to the
Establishment of New Departments Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. There they have been joined by various resource an energy responsibilities from the ministries of industry and trade and commerce. In the government organization bill all these will be fashioned to form a single department of energy, mines and resources. There will be one minister who will have both the facilities to develop and the authority to implement national policies with regard to the resource and energy responsibilities of the federal government with the exception of resource development in northern territories.
Resources and energy are, of course, closely inter-related. Energy, on the one hand, is the product of resource use; it is on the other, a key to the full application and use of our resources generally and we believe it is wise to have the two handled together if policy is to be of the greatest effectiveness and to contribute to our long term economic growth and development. The new organization will greatly facilitate this.
A totally different but no less vital instrument in the order growth and development of the Canadian society is the law itself. In this connection the government organization bill is concerned with re-shaping the Department of Justice and the Department of the Secretary of State, with raising the office of the Solicitor General to departmental status and with the establishment of a department of government, the department of the registrar general, which will bring together legislation and policy concerning existing federal responsibility for certain aspects of business activity.
In recent years governments have been much concerned with social legislation which has involved the establishment of economic mechanisms to achieve national purposes. All of this has enormously increased the burdens upon our law officers and legal advisers. It has also caused us to think more readily in terms of economic rather than strictly legal techniques for encouraging social action. In administering these techniques, under the present set-up we have tended to overload our legal advisers. This has resulted in a tendency to obscure the creative social role which the law itself can perform. It is in the context of correcting both these failings that the government organization bill will propose the completion of a radical reform of the Crown's law offices.
On the one hand, the Department of Justice and the office of the Attorney General of
May 9. 1968

Establishment of New Departments Canada will be returned to the lull time discharge of their traditional functions: the drafting of legislation and documents; the conduct of litigation and prosecutions. The appointment and maintenance of courts and quasi-judicial tribunals will rest here, where principle of justice and the lessons of history show they should reside. The R.C.M.P., criminal investigations, detentions, paroles and pardons, on the other hand, will be the full time responsibility of the Solicitor General in a department which, like the Home Office in Britain, will be separate and distinct from that of the Attorney General.
In addition to the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General the government organization bill will provide for a third department, the Department of the registrar general, which will have charge of that aspect of legislation dealing with what might be called business law. Patents, trade marks, companies, bankruptcy and restrictive trade practices are all matters which have important economic as well as legal aspects. Legislation in these areas must not merely record commercial rights but protect the national interest and the rights of individuals and act as an instrument in the promotion of social and economic goals.
Hon. members will have noted that some of the areas of business law which I mentioned will be taken from the Department of the Secretary of State. The work transferred from this department will certainly be replaced by the transfer to it of the citizenship branch of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. The government organization bill will seek the repeal of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration Act after making provision for the transfer of citizenship responsibilities to the Secretary of State. I am sure that this change will commend itself.

So these matters will all be in the Secretary of State's department.
A further feature of the bill that is of no small importance is the implementation of

the recommendation of the Glassco commission to put the Treasury Board under a separate minister.

This is by no means the case and it would not be wise to consider that any reorganization, however extensive, and this is certainly an extensive one, is final.
The Royal Commission on Government Organization, the Glassco Commission, noted as found on page 26, volume 5 of its report:
The persistence of change and the need for adjustment to change are, in fact, the only future certainties known to any organization. The successful adaptation of the machinery of government to changing circumstances will require two things: within the public service itself there must be an awareness that adaptation is an inescapable part of the task of management: and, both within the public service and beyond it, there must be a continuous assessment of the role of the federal government in the life of Canada, to ensure that the machinery of government remains responsive to the ends it must serve.
As the circumstances of society change in this swift-changing, indeed, revolutionary age, the pattern of governmental organization and of administrative direction must also change if they are to be properly effective. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that in this resolution

Speaking seriously, Mr. Chairman, is it not a terrible mess? The cornerstone of reform omitted. The powers of reaction apparently have become paramount in the government. I may make reference to this a little later, but I wish to assure you at once that anything we on this side of the house can do to preserve the Minister of Forestry from oblivion among his colleagues will be done. If the Prime Minister will bring in a resolution to include the unincluded, I think we could pass it pretty well unanimously without further discussion and thereby present more proof that an opposition can be beneficial.
The government has produced a resolution which, to say the least, shows that the Prime Minister has forgotten he has in his ranks a man of reform and vision. Indeed, he has been so far in advance of those with whom he serves that often there has been wonder how he got into that party at all. With reference to the resolution the Prime Minister dealt at some length with the necessity of improving the organization of government. No one disputes the necessity for that, but reforms based on experiment and not experience do not always work out very well. We had an example of that in connection with the committee system. Two years ago or a year and a half ago I said we were going much too far under our form of government in bringing about the United States idea of a
[Mr. Diefenbaker.I
committee system. What have we found? We have found that the government cannot get its members to attend. Committees are set up and they are not being attended. This is another example of what befalls a government which just tries to do something new regardless of how experimental the plan may be.
What is the situation today? There are 127 or 128 members on the government side of the house including 26 ministers and 16 parliamentary secretaries. Thirty per cent of the membership occupy positions of responsibility. But with all that horde, Mr. Chairman, they come up with a resolution which omits one of the major considerations, the assurance that agriculture shall receive a fair deal. It indicates that this government has forgotten agriculture. It is very obvious that this government no longer considers agriculture of any great consequence.
The government is increasing the number of ministers. It is shuffling the deck and adding a couple more deuces; that is what is happening. The trend today in parliamentary systems in other parts of the world is not to increase the number of ministers but to reduce them. I know how difficult that is, but today the cabinet is too large for the effective carrying out of the business of the nation. If he were to call together only certain members of the cabinet, the Prime Minister would have difficulty. Preferences naturally would be assumed.
I think one of the major reforms which must be brought about is to ensure a reduction in the number of ministers and to divide those ministers into two classifications, those of the cabinet and those of the ministry. It will be difficult to do, but if there is to be any effective reform of cabinet government, that is the first thing which must be done. I recognize all of the difficulties. As I look at this shuffling, I wonder what were the reasons.
I have here the original press conference statement made by the Prime Minister on December 17 in which he sets out the benefits which will flow from these changes. I am going to summarize it. He said that the changes were designed to adapt the machinery of the government to new and changing needs. He further said that the planned changes were designed to improve efficiency by increasing the attention given to the problems that have become more important. Those conditions become significant when we realize that agricultural rehabilitation has
May 9, 1966	COMMONS
been left out in the cold. In his press release the Prime Minister went on to say:
At present some of the most important problems of government are the concern of only one section of a department, while others are scattered among various departments and agencies. The effect of the administrative changes will be that one minister will have a specific responsibility for the Treasury Board-
I think that is a good move; I think it is necessary. On the basis of personal experience I think that one deserves implementation.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Let us look at the others. Resources have been divided, part going to the minister of Indian affairs and northern development and part going to the minister of energy, mines and resources. Why should some of our resources be placed under one department and others under another? How does one obtain strength by division?
Labour has been divided with the Minister of Labour responsible for legislation on collective bargaining and other things in that field and the minister of manpower responsible for training, placement and immigration. The Prime Minister suggested that this was a forward step but I think it is a retrograde one which represents the antitheses of the recommendation, as I read it, of Woods, Gordon and Company which made a report on this subject in November, 1965. After all, this is one of the leading companies of chartered accountants and consultants in Canada, and no matter how you look at the situation the hon. member for Davenport, who was connected with this firm at one time, was a man with ideas. Sometimes I wonder how the "Gordon Highlanders" are going to be able to stand up to the "Sharpshooters".
In any event, this recommendation was ignored and I should like to know why it was ignored. The recommendation reads as follows;
The manpower and labour relations fields have in the past been regarded as being largely unrelated. However it is becoming increasingly evident that in the type of industrial society toward which we appear to be heading, manpower problems will, to a greater and greater extent, become labour relations problems as well. As the pace of technological change quickens, so must the adjustments to change quicken, and in this situation workers will look increasingly to the institution of collective bargaining to ensure that their interests are adequately protected. Management, on the other hand, will be seeking to negotiate the elimination or modification of contract provisions that are making it difficult to adapt to change or are standing in the way of rational solutions to manpower adjustment problems. The conclusion we draw from

Establishment of New Departments this is that, although the manpower and labour relations fields are distinct, there are increasingly important interactions between them. This suggests that the development of policy and programs in these two fields must continue to be closely integrated.
Integrated policies do not result from divided responsibilities among ministers. I wonder why that recommendation was not carried into effect.
It is interesting to note how the changes took place. According to the press there was a great internal power dispute last November and December over the suggestion that members of the cabinet from the province of Quebec should be given prestige appointments. New oil was poured into old bottles. The three wise men were brought in and each one of them is ambitious. I do not criticize ambition, but what did this bring about? It brought about a hodgepodge.
The minister of energy, mines and resources, who carries on temporarily as the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, will take over the responsibility for atomic energy, oil, gas and water power, and water and coal. I have already dealt with the duties of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and the authority that he is going to have as minister of manpower.
These men had to be given decorative authority. After all, they wanted them to have prestige. I read the French language press each day and it has been said there that the great weakness of the former cabinet resulted from the fact there were not enough prestige appointments for the province of Quebec. Prestige has now been created by giving these new decorative powers to these members from the province of Quebec. I am not going into the events that took place when the President of the Privy Council was minister of justice, but he is the one now who is going to be looking after the administration of the Bankruptcy Act. He had that responsibility when he was the minister of justice and bankruptcies multiplied three, four or fivefold. There is also a strange situation regarding combines legislation.
Apparently it was felt that everybody should have something added and the plan was to build people up in this way because they did not want to occupy small portfolios such as that of Secretary of State. Now these people will have more authority and greater new power. This is termed by the government a measure to strengthen administration
May 9, 19G6

Establishment of New Departments but I suggest the purpose behind this measure is to strengthen the present administration.
The situation with regard to the Department of Justice is the most interesting of all. All that minister now has is the name. I presume he will be very effective in carrying out his duties because the government has taken away the whole essence of the Department of Justice. How can one have a Department of Justice with authority spread out all over the place?
I am very much impressed with the way the Solicitor General answers questions in the house and accepts his responsibility, but what do we now find the situation to be in that department? The Solicitor General has practically appropriated the major powers of the Department of Justice. All the Minister of Justice is going to have left is the prestige of the name. Apparently he is to look after legal matters in the Department of Justice. That looks all right on the face of it, but what legal matters come to the attention of the Minister of Justice? He is not in the position of having such things come to his attention because the law officers of the Crown look after these various things: The government had to keep him in the cabinet so it continued his title, realizing no doubt that it might be better to place his authority elsewhere.
The administrative changes mean nothing. With one or two exceptions they seem in large measure to be designed to enable the Prime Minister to take care of his commitments. Instead of cabinet posts being created in accordance with departmental needs they seem to have been created in accordance with the political needs of the government. The divided and subdivided powers of the Department of Justice can only result in indifferent administration and confusion One can see today in Ottawa a lack of confidence on the part of professional civil servants who observe departments being splintered, severed and added to other departments for what has every appearance of being a political purpose on the part of the government. That is not good enough because administrative necessity is not met by conforming to political necessity.
Whenever questions are directed to the Minister of Labour answers are given, as is the case in respect of questions directed to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, in keeping with the responsibilities of the government. However, certain

powers are to be taken from that hon. gentleman and I have already mentioned some of those in connection with the proposed changes in the Department of Labour.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
What about agriculture? We cannot discuss that because it is not even before us. But we were told in advance, months ago, what was going to be done. They had to give something to the Minister of Forestry. When we set up the Department of Forestry it was ridiculed and laughed at. They had to give the Minister of Forestry something to give him prestige. What is the use of being a reformer without prestige? But what a position for a minister to be in-forgotten, only remembered for what he has done. I hope this situation will be corrected at the earliest possible date so that our uncertainty and concern will be obliterated
May I say that if ARDA has been included in the responsibilities of the Minister of Forestry it would have meant and will mean that agriculture is being placed in a secondary position. When I mentioned this a while ago I noticed one of the ministers indicating disapproval, so I shall read from the Family Herald, a magazine nationally and internationally known, what is said on the question of the alteration in portfolio responsibilities:
We were disappointed that there has yet been no indication as to how these all-embracing portfolios will be dovetailed with the existing ministries which cover rural development and agriculture. For despite the reverse title there appears to be no apparent change in Mr. Sauve's responsibilities. And we cannot help but feel that the ministry of agriculture has been relegated to a secondary status, comprising the ill-defined policies under the direction of a little-known minister.
Agriculture is placed in a secondary position. Why? The Prime Minister when he was leader of the opposition said, "We have to have two ministers of agriculture, a western minister and an eastern minister." One of the ministers had already appropriated to himself the position of eastern minister of agriculture but he never got the portfolio because it was not set up. Agriculture, as the Family Herald says, is relegated to a secondary position.
What reforms are there? There is a Treasury Board minister. That is a forward step and a necessary one. But you have agriculture placed in a tertiary position. It is not even included in the resolution. They have forgotten about it altogether in this resolution which took a long time for a government that was most careful in assuring that everything would be included to prepare.
May 9. 1966

Yet they forgot about agriculture. You have a minister of manpower to be. He has a wide knowledge of labour problems, and in regard to his manner of approach in the House of Commons I say to him that I like the way in which he places his views before the house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: But what do we see? Labour problems are handed to one minister and then another. How can this minister be effective? Surely we have not arrived at the point where the government contends that to make this important department effective it has to be divided and subdivided by spreading out responsibility. Certainly labour problems are of major importance, but why the subdivision? I come back to the reason. They wanted everybody to have something so that one minister and another could say, "He got this but I got that." But in it all the Minister of Forestry became the forgotten man. I would not allow that. That is why I would draw this matter to the attention of the house, because we will not have a minister removed by governmental forgetfulness. It cannot be permitted. I hope the Prime Minister will seize on this problem and without delay remove the fear that fills our hearts that this minister, so necessary in the new politics is to be left out.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the Prime Minister has said, this resolution forecasts legislation which will constitute a fairly extensive reorganization of the various departments of government. Some of the reorganization proposed in the resolution we believe is advisable and indeed long overdue. Other parts of the reorganization we would want to reserve judgment on until we have had an opportunity to see the legislation itself.
I am somewhat surprised that the resolution introduced by the Prime Minister would seem to indicate that there is to be a single measure covering all the various items which he outlined. The government knows its own course of action best, but it seems to me that a single piece of legislation including all these
Establishment of New Departments various measures will cause a great deal of confusion in the future. It is much tidier for a department to have an act setting out those matters with which it may deal and the powers of the minister, those things he may do by ministerial discretion, by regulation through the governor in council and so on. Then, if the new department finds, as it will find, that certain of its powers need to be amended, altered or extended, the act can be amended from time to time. If the department goes into a hodgepodge with a number of other departments for which there is a single piece of legislation, the government will find itself in some difficulty. Perhaps the government has in mind that this will be an interim measure and individual acts will be introduced separately at a later date. But I do suggest to the government that unless later they separate the legislation in respect of these departments they will find themselves in a great deal of departmental difficulty.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I agree with what the Prime Minister said about the importance of giving thought to this question of government reorganization. Too often members of parliament and the public generally think that administration is not really important and that it does not make much difference what kind of departments we have. As a matter of fact, clearcut allocations of responsibility, a clear line of authority for the discharge of that responsibility and clearly defined lines of communication are absolutely essential in the complex society in which we live if government policies are to be carried out effectively and efficiently.
I should like to deal briefly with a few of the matters which the Prime Minister has suggested the legislation will implement. The first is the setting up of a department of manpower. In addition to its role for the training and allocation of manpower and job placement, it will also have some of the functions now pertaining to immigration. I believe this is an excellent combination. It seems to me that the body which is responsible for keeping its finger on the economic pulse and being fully aware of the manpower needs of the country is in the best position to deal with immigration, to know what number of people we can allow into Canada at any one time, to know what skills they should have or, if they do not have any skills, what training they will need after they come to Canada. Therefore I think the combination of immigration and manpower is excellent.
May 9, 1966

Establishment of New Departments
The Economic Council of Canada recommended, of course, that this combination be carried out and I am very glad that the government has seen fit to do so. If I may say so to the Prime Minister, I believe that both the minister and the deputy minister who have been selected for this department are admirable choices. I believe they are both equipped in terms of training and temperament to take on what will be a very difficult task which will involve blazing new trails and working out new programs. However, I want to say to the Prime Minister that if this manpower department, which our party has been recommending for years, is to be modelled on the Swedish labour market board and is really to have the kind of function which a manpower department should have in a technological society, it will require a great deal of support in terms of money and trained personnel. If the manpower program is to be more than a paper program there will have to be a very large sum of money spent on the training and retraining of workers as well as on the upgrading of their education.
I had some opportunity to see at first hand the work of the labour market board in Sweden. Of course, they have been at it for a long time, but they spend tremendous sums of money in training and retraining workers and as a result they are making full utilization of all their available manpower. This is something which we are not doing in Canada. The Economic Council of Canada has stated that we have now come within 97 per cent of our productive capacity. We are not using men and women in Canada who are often unskilled and unemployed and who will have to be retrained. Many of them will have to have their educational qualifications upgraded. There is no sense in giving the minister and his department, with all their enthusiasm, this heavy responsibility unless the government is also prepared to give them the very large sums of money necessary to carry out an effective program.
All I want to say about the responsibility given to the Solicitor General is that I believe it is a good thing to have the minister charged with the responsibility for penitentiaries. There has been a great deal of talk about penal reform in this House of Commons but very little has ever been done about it.
I believe that there should be a minister charged with the responsibility for looking into law reform, and the overhaul of the Criminal Code, and these other matters can


very well be given to the Solicitor General. However, whether the R.C.M.P. should be separated from the department charged with the responsibility for law enforcement is something about which I have some doubts. My colleague, the hon. member for Greenwood, will probably discuss this in more detail later.
I congratulate the government for combining the Indian affairs branch with northern development; I believe this is a natural affinity. I have complained for years that Indian affairs have usually been under the jurisdiction of civil servants who have never seen an Indian in broad daylight and have never seen an Eskimo except on television. I know that with the combination now being proposed the Indians will be served by people who are much more familiar with their problems and the solutions for these problems.
With reference to the proposed department of the registrar general which the Prime Minister suggested is to deal with business law and those things which affect the protection of the nation and individuals, I think this is a very helpful move. We in the New Democratic Party have been advocating for years the setting up of a department of consumer affairs. We are still hopeful that the government will see its way clear to set up such a department. We would like to see the department charged with the responsibility for administering combines investigation legislation and restrictive trade practices legislation greatly strengthened with some teeth in that legislation.
We would like to see provision for the standardization of weights and packaging, with legislation to prevent misleading advertising. We would like, as we have said on many occasions, to see such a department have a price review board with full authority to look into price increases to see whether or not they are fully justified by increases in costs. We are convinced that such an investigation would show in some cases that increases in prices are warranted but in other cases it would show that they are not warranted.
Action by any company or combination of companies to raise prices merely to take advantage of a situation would receive a good deal of public criticism and if the criticism became widespread enough, of course, the federal and provincial governments would find it necessary to pass concurrent legislation to deal' with these price increases. My own opinion is that no such legislation would
May 9, 1966

become necessary because the exposure to public gaze of unconscionable profiteering would be enough to correct the situation. If the government is not going to set up a department of consumer affairs, then certainly the kind of department the Prime Minister proposed today could be the nucleus around which a department of consumer affairs could be built. I hope that if time permits my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, will elaborate on this question because it is something to which she has given a great deal of thought and about which she is very enthusiastic.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Finally, I want to say a word or two about the proposed president of the Treasury Board. Again, I agree with this proposal. I hope that in the not too distant future the Prime Minister will appoint a minister to give his full time to the responsibilities of being president of the Treasury Board. I should like to see the Treasury Board working on two functions which are not assigned to it at the present time. First, I think the Treasury Board ought to have a branch which would act as a budget bureau. At the present time, we have a Treasury Board which allocates funds according to departments and subdivides them according to branches. We have an Auditor General who audits the expenditures of these agencies. However, there is no agency for auditing the performance of departments and branches; there is no agency to examine the programs to see whether they still fill a useful function or whether they should be curtailed or even eliminated.
Every member knows that Parkinson's law operates in every government. Consequently, from time to time we set up commissions like the Glassco Commission which report to the government on whatever extravagance, duplication, overstaffing and unnecessary procedures are found. The tragedy is that by the time a government, not necessarily this government but any government, gets around to dealing with the situation which has been described by the commission the situation itself has altered. The only effective way that a government can deal with the problem of the proliferation of staff, extravagance and waste is to have a continuing agency constantly examining departments, constantly going over their programs to see whether or not those programs are still useful and whether or not the department is still using
Establishment of New Departments its staff efficiently or is asking for more money than the service which they render warrants. Every member knows that no program, once having started, is ever voluntarilj curtailed by those who are running it.
Every minister and every deputy minister is told by his branch head that a program is absolutely necessary. A program may have been started 30 years ago to meet a certain situation and the situation may have changed, but the program has to be kept going. If the government is really going to do an effective job of eliminating waste and extravagance. I think they need something resembling the United States budget bureau. I can remember an instance when I was associated with a provincial administration. A certain department was asking for more money, more staff and more space. This meant putting up new buildings. The department alleged it was so crowded, so understaffed and working in quarters so congested they were not doing effective work. They made a marvellous case for a lot more money, a lot more space and a lot more people. When the budget bureau had investigated the case for over six months they found that by a simplification of procedures, by amending the filing systems, they could move some of the staff to other departments. Then, by microfilming their records, we were able to get rid of hundreds of file cabinets which resulted in more floor space.
Unless you have an agency to do this the staff keeps growing, the space required keeps increasing, the demands for larger and larger estimates keep rolling in to the Treasury Board. It seems to me one of the functions that ought to be given to this Treasury Board branch would be the assignment of teams to any department that is asking for more money to conduct an investigation. Even if the department is not asking for more money, perhaps it is getting too much money now. A team of experts could be sent to examine the procedures, to analyse the program and make a report to the Treasury Board whether or not this department was getting enough money or too much money, whether it could reduce staff and get along with a smaller allocation of funds.
The other function I should like to see given to the president of the Treasury Board is related to the whole basis of economic planning. I am trying to fit within the government's framework something I had hoped the government would do. Personally I would prefer to see a department of economic affairs and planning, an agency which could
May 9, 1966

Establishment of New Departments work closely with the Treasury Board, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Industry and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Since the government has not set up a department of economics affairs and planning, it seems to me that the Treasury Board could form the nucleus for the beginning of a genuine economic planning agency.
So far as I can see at the moment, there is no real economic planning in the government's set-up. The Economic Council, which I understand has been moved now from the Secretary of State to the Prime Minister's office, is purely an advisory body and does not concern itself with day to day planning. It is doing long term projections and is doing excellent work. I want to congratulate the chairman and members of the Economic Council on the two reviews they have published. They are amongst the best things that have been put out in Canada and the council should be encouraged to continue.
However, the council works in one office and the Treasury Board works in another office. The Department of Industry works separately, as does the Department of Trade and Commerce. I know the Prime Minister will tell me there is a cabinet committee that co-ordinates the work of these various departments. I do not believe cabinet committees can do this. I think the members of such committees are too busy. I am sure they do not meet often enough. I am sure when they do meet they have even greater trouble in getting a quorum than have the committees of the House of Commons because these men are very busy and are called all over the country.
If there is going to be any real economic planning, any real co-ordination of economic activities, it has to start at a lower level. It is not going to be done or to be very effective if it is not, and for that reason it seems to be some thought should be given-

That was not bad economic planning; that is just poor timing. It seems to me some thought ought to be given to having in the Treasury Board the Economic Council of Canada and representatives from the Department of Industry as well as Trade and Commerce co-ordinated so that within the Treasury Board itself there could be the nucleus of a genuine economic planning agency. [DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
It seems to me that until this kind of economic planning is done we are going to continue to have what we now have, namely, a lot of competing departments all asking treasury for money, with the Minister of Finance and members of the Treasury Board having to slash requests each year when making up the budget. Often the estimates have to be reduced not by any order of priority but because the departments are told to take their estimates back and cut off 15 per cent in order to bring expenditure into line with revenue. This is a most unscientific way to reduce estimates. Some departments may have more money than they need. Others do not have enough. The sort of thing I contemplate can only be done if we build the kind of fiscal and economic planning agency that will enable the cabinet to make the kind of informed decisions which will help this country to grow and prosper.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, we are glad that the government is bringing in some of these measures for reorganization. We may have doubts about some of the details. We shall be able to discuss those more intelligently when we see the legislation. In the meantime we commend the government for taking several very important forward steps in the resolution which has been presented today.

I disagree with the Prime Minister if the final conclusion to be drawn from his initial

It seems to me that one of the problems we face today is that we are yielding to the pressures by following the path of least resistance, which too often results in things being taken over by the authority of the government. I am concerned, therefore, that at the present time we have the prospect of even greater control through federal government adminidministra-tion. However, if the object of this government reorganization is to decrease government interference and government control over Canadians while at the same time facilitating greater efficiency and effectiveness of government, then we completely support the resolution.
I think it is high time that more recommendations of the Glassco Commission were instituted. I am concerned that we have already waited far too long to implement many of the obvious recommendations. As a result, if I sense correctly what is happening within the civil service at the present time, there is a general state of confusion and uncertainty which has resulted from these now very rapid and extensive changes in the structure of the federal government.
I believe it is vital, Mr. Chairman, that there be very well defined and clearcut areas of responsibility so far as governmental departments are concerned and that in this connection there be a complete flow of information to facilitate communication between governmental departments. None of these changes that are now contemplated will reach their desired objectives unless this is so. It seems to me that the transfer of certain responsibilities from the Minister of Justice to the Solicitor General might be very useful and increase the efficiency as well as the effectiveness of the administration of justice. It is also my opinion that it is a very sound idea to set up ministry of manpower. One of the greatest problems we face in Canada today concerns the question of manpower. We boast about a booming economy; yet this very month there are 340,000 people who are unemployed. This emphasizes the fact that re-education is vital 
if we are to make best use of our work force. It is a paradox that so many people should be unemployed in an economy which is in some areas looking for skilled labour.
It is important that the government should recognize immigration as an important factor in any manpower policy. The greatest eras of prosperity in our history have come in times when we have received the greatesl influx of new immigrants. A complete overhaul of the department of immigration is necessary and it is logical that this should be combined with a vocational training program of wide scope so as to develop essential additional sources of skilled labour.
The effects of automation in Canada are proving to be different from those which had been anticipated. For a number of years we are unlikely to be faced with any real problem so far as automation is concerned because of the tremendous scope which exists for the development of our resources. Nevertheless there is need for a continuing assessment of this situation and a department of manpower appears to be the logical answer so far as government organization is concerned.
I am somewhat concerned to find that the Department of Labour is being emasculated, as it were, by the setting up of the proposed department of manpower. However, I would assume there will be an opportunity for greater emphasis on industrial relations and a more harmonious labour situation across Canada so far as the federal administration is concerned, particularly in the field of co-ordination between federal and provincial departments of labour. The importance of this question will continue to increase. From information I have it seems to me that co-operation between the various departments of labour will become more feasible under the arrangement proposed.

Mr. Chairman, resolution No. 56 concerns a government project to establish five new government departments.
The resolution stipulates that:
It is expedient to introduce a measure respecting the organization of the government of Canada_
Does this mean that the government is disorganized? The question is obvious.
-to establish a Department of the Solicitor General, Department of Manpower, Department of the Registrar General. Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and Department of Energy, Mines and Resources;-
And, of course, to establish at the same time the bureaucracy and the bunch of bureaucrats necessary to all these departments.

The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) has just mentioned that, under the circumstances, it would have been quite expedient to establish a Department of Federal-Provincial Affairs, because anyone who sees this list of new departments can tell that three of them will undoubtedly be directly concerned with questions under the jurisdiction of the provinces. For example, there will be a department of manpower. The provinces, whether Quebec or British Columbia, do not want their course of action or their policy to be dictated by the federal government.
The provincial authorities rightly believe that the matter of manpower comes under their jurisdiction and, in Quebec, we believe this sincerely and deeply.
With regard to Indian affairs and northern development, we witnessed in this house negotiations which took place between the present Minister of Northern Affairs of the province of Quebec, then Minister of Natural Resources, and the federal Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
The minister of the provincial government maintained that the administration of Indian affairs belonged to Quebec, as far as northern Quebec was concerned, and the federal minister held the opposite view.
Today, the government is asking the house to pass the resolution to establish a department of Indian affairs and northern development. That will create conflicts between the provinces and the Canadian government.
The establishment of a department of energy, mines and resources is also proposed. We saw the government of British Columbia and the federal government, then headed by the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Die-fenbaker), engaged in a rather fierce struggle which lasted four, five, even six years. When the federal government of the day toppled, we saw the same struggle continue between the government of British Columbia and the present federal government; finally a compromise was reached under which the claims of the government of British Columbia to the effect that mines, resources and energy come under provincial jurisdiction were recognized.
In the present circumstances, Mr. Chairman, forever increasing the number of ministers, or appointing five more, does not seem to me the way to solve the problems which are now facing the Canadian economy and which the Canadian people must now overcome.
